chapter_theme: Knowing the assembly (அவையறிதல்): where learning should be spoken and before whom. The worthy keep silent before the ignorant and the quarrelsome, while those who memorise texts without understanding them expose themselves. A book's meaning is harder than its letter, and only those who can explain it, by the full method of commentary, count as scholars.
structure_note: 311 to 316 describe the bad assembly and the false scholar: the ignorant who spread error, the rote reciter who turns to abuse and violence, the itching debater, the brawler. 317 to 319 turn to books: the distance between text and meaning, the collector and the explainer, and what a commentary must do. 320 ends with good birth as the source of a restrained tongue.

311.reading: Before people of dark understanding, who leave the way of an assembly of true knowledge, put forward some piece of ignorance, spread it everywhere and live by petty learning, let the wise leave their wisdom unspoken.
311.nuance: The advice is silence, not argument. Mudaliar records another reading of கைஞ்ஞானம் as 'skill of the hand', the habit of striking whoever objects, which would anticipate 312 and 315.

312.reading: The disciplined keep away from the bad scholar who recites lessons by rote as if he knew their beauty; worsted in the assembly he will abuse their family, or else slap his shoulders and rise to fight.
312.nuance: Pope calls the தீப்புலவன் a heretic, the teacher of an evil system. Mudaliar's gloss is simply one without learning, and Shanmuganar's a false poet. The danger here is social: the loser turns to insult and violence.

313.reading: Many people talk at length: they itch to rise and debate on the strength of a word, cannot judge the power of learning, do not know how to make what they learned reach the hearer, and do not know when they are beaten.
313.nuance: Mudaliar gives several ways to divide the opening words, one of them 'with words for goads', which Shanmuganar follows. The last failure, not knowing defeat, is what keeps the talk going.

314.reading: With no learning of his own, a fool picks up a single sutra by overhearing a teacher's lesson, then walks unabashed into a gathering of the good, recites it, and shows how petty his understanding is.
314.nuance: Mudaliar specifies that the fool has only the bare text (மூல பாடம்) of the sutra, overheard from lessons given to other students.

315.reading: Those who join people who rage and burn like beasts for the sake of victory and will not accept the truth, and who rise among them to show off their eloquence, will see their own teeth in their hands like gourd seeds.
315.nuance: Mudaliar names the figure: teeth in the hand say, without saying it, that they will be knocked out. The warning falls on the speaker who chooses that company, not on the brawlers.

316.reading: When fools who only recite the text and cannot make out its meaning say things that provoke anger, the worthy, whose renown does not decay, stand ashamed and grieve deeply for the mother who bore them.
316.nuance: The shame belongs to the listeners, not the fool. Mudaliar quotes the kind of lament the worthy might make, that she bore him for others to laugh at, and names the figure as imputed cause.

317.reading: Books are easy for anyone who learns them in due order, like the shoulders of women who take whatever they are paid, but their meaning is hard for anyone to grasp, like the minds of those same women with skin like tender mango shoots.
317.nuance: One simile does both halves of the work: access to the text is cheap and open, and understanding is closed. Pope's 'sacred texts' narrows நூல், which the commentators leave general.

318.reading: Some collect books in great numbers and fill the whole house with them without understanding what they say; the scholars who keep books are one kind, and those who understand them and make others understand are another.
318.nuance: Shanmuganar takes போற்றும் as keeping the books with worship (பூசை போட்டு) and calls the keepers false scholars. The verse itself says only that they are a different kind.

319.reading: Lord of the long hills where herds of wild cattle gather, can the words of those who do not sift a faultless work through the four modes of summary, breadth, subtlety and remainder, and so show its full extent, be a good commentary on it?
319.nuance: A quatrain about commentary, on whose terms its commentators disagree. Mudaliar adds that others define the four modes differently again.

positions.position: The four are a method of disputation: breadth raises objections, subtlety answers them, and the remainder states the conclusion they establish.
positions.quote: எச்சவுரையாவது இவ்வாறு தடைவிடைகளான் முடிந்த ஒரு பொருளை யுரைத்தல்.

positions.position: The remainder is research that brings out what lies hidden and unsaid in the text.
positions.quote: நூலில் எஞ்சி மறைந்து கிடப்பதை எடுத்துக்கூறும் ஆராய்ச்சியுரை

320.reading: However many books they learn, can those not born of a good house be the means of guarding others' words? And the well-born wise take no notice of the petty understanding of those who do not grasp the books they talk of.
320.nuance: Pope offers a third reading of the first half: guarding others from faults of speech. The second half fits Mudaliar's reading best, since the well-born show the restraint the first half denies to the low-born by overlooking a fool's errors.

positions.position: Those of low birth lack the restraint needed to protect others' words from scorn.
Those of low birth cannot protect and care for others by what they say.
positions.quote: தம் சொல்லால், பிறரைப் போற்றிக் காக்கத்தக்க கருவி போன்றிருப்பரோ?

links.note: Both tell those who speak well in a good assembly not to speak in a mean one; 311 describes the mean assembly in detail.
312 warns that the bad scholar will rise to fight; 315 shows the cost to whoever stays to argue: his teeth in his hand.
649 says those who cannot say a few faultless words long to say many; 313 shows the same many-worded speaker in debate.
403 says even the unlearned are good if they stay silent before the learned; 314's fool fails at exactly that.
857 says those of bitter understanding who hold to hostility do not see the truth that brings victory; 315's disputants want victory and will not accept the truth (மெய் கொள்ளார்).
In 69 a mother rejoices more than at his birth when she hears her son called சான்றோன். In 316 the சான்றோர் themselves grieve for the mother of a fool. The two verses are mirror images.
317 separates a book's text from its meaning; 318 separates those who keep the text from those who grasp the meaning and teach it.
650 likens those who cannot explain what they learned to flowers without scent; 318 sets them apart from scholars who make others understand.
318 says true scholars make a book's meaning clear to others; 319 sets out what that explanation must contain.

409 says the learned of low birth have a worth the unlearned of high birth lack. 320 says that however much they learn, those without good birth cannot do what the well-born do. The conflict depends on reading இற்பிறப்பு as birth into a good family, as both commentators do, and on counting the capacity 320 denies as part of the worth 409 gives to learning.
992 makes birth in a good family one of the two parts of courtesy; 320 credits good birth with the restraint to overlook another's petty understanding.

source_issues: Quatrain 311: Pope's translation is not aligned.
Quatrain 316: the Tamil prints முடர் for மூடர். Shanmuganar's commentary opens with a stray பொதுவியல் and reads வாளர் இருப்பர், apparently for வாளா இருப்பர்.
Quatrain 317: the Tamil has a garbled character in அறிதற் கா஢ய, which Mudaliar's gloss (அருமையானவை) shows to be அரிய.
Quatrain 320: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of chapter 33 and the opening line of quatrain 321.
